claim: In parent/child architectural dev work, the user does not delegate understanding to the agent: the user must stay on-the-loop at every depth of nested work, and a new depth level cannot arise without the user's participation in creating it.

evidence.detail: Source statement: sub-agents insulate the user from interfacing with and monitoring the sub-agent, which both prevents intervention and acts as a deferment of understanding. The user delegates things that, in conceptual architecture work, should not be delegated - the nuance of architecture often lives in the implementation details. A research survey confirmed the anti-pattern has names in the literature (cognitive atrophy, the augmentation trap, deferred understanding) and that published multi-agent patterns all retain some delegation-of-understanding.

Atomization migration (plans/atomize): claim restated to the norm; enumerable content moved to invariants. Descriptive rationale extracted to atoms cb:b820, cb:b821, now deps. Previous claim: In parent/child architectural dev work, the user does not delegate understanding to the agent. The user must stay on-the-loop at every depth of nested work. This is what distinguishes parent/child structure from sub-agent delegation, which abstracts in-progress reasoning away from the user and forecloses intervention. A new depth level cannot arise without the user's participation in creating it. Maps onto an operations/engineering mode split: in operational work, delegation is fine (bounded, mechanical work); in architectural work, delegation breaks the user's ability to audit the reasoning that produces architectural decisions.
